task.swarm_objective: Assess how the AI semiconductor supply chain (foundry, custom silicon, memory, server CPUs) is benefiting from AI demand, using recent filings and earnings information.
task.agent_directive: Investigate Micron's high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and data-center memory revenue driven by AI demand, with cited figures.
constraints: Cite a source for every financial figure you record.
Use the most recently reported fiscal periods.
Focus on HBM and data-center memory.
success_criteria: Report HBM or data-center revenue figures for recent quarters

tool_arguments.query: Micron HBM revenue Q3 fiscal 2025 AI demand

events.content: Micron HBM revenue Q3 fiscal 2025 AI demand

Micron did not disclose a stand-alone total HBM-revenue figure for fiscal Q3 2026; it did disclose that it had already shipped **more than $1 billion of HBM4 revenue**, while HBM4 12-high’s volume ramp was running about twice as fast as the prior HBM3E 12-high ramp. [[1]] 

The broader AI-memory read-through was exceptionally strong: fiscal Q3 revenue was **$41.46 billion**, including record DRAM revenue of **$31.3 billion** (76% of sales, +67% sequentially) and NAND revenue of **$9.9 billion** (+99% sequentially). [[2]] [[3]] 

Data-center revenue exceeded **$25 billion** in the quarter—an annualized run rate above $100 billion—and data-center SSD revenue exceeded **$5 billion**, more than doubling sequentially. [[3]] 

Management attributed the tight market to AI-driven demand, saying DRAM and NAND industry demand continued to significantly exceed supply and that it expected tight conditions to persist beyond calendar 2027. [[3]] 

The demand outlook also strengthened because Micron raised its calendar-2026 server-unit-growth expectation to the **high-teens percentage range**, citing agentic AI’s expansion of memory needs beyond accelerator racks into CPU and storage infrastructure. [[3]] 

For forward visibility, Micron said it had entered 16 strategic customer agreements, with approximately **$100 billion** of remaining performance obligations for agreements signed through and after fiscal Q3, although it cautioned that RPO is based on minimum committed volumes/prices and is not a forecast of total revenue. [[3]] 

In short, the reported **>$1 billion HBM4 figure** confirms a rapid early ramp, while the much larger data-center, DRAM, pricing, supply-tightness, and contracted-demand disclosures indicate that AI demand was the central driver of Micron’s fiscal-Q3 surge rather than HBM alone. [[1]] [[3]]

Sources:
[S1.1] Financial results - Micron Investor Relations — https://investors.micron.com/static-files/2354ecda-77a0-4ddd-8462-a631eb491356
[S1.2] Micron Technology, Inc. - Micron Technology, Inc. Reports Record Results for the Third Quarter of Fiscal 2026 — https://investors.micron.com/news/press-release/2026/Micron-Technology-Inc--Reports-Record-Results-for-the-Third-Quarter-of-Fiscal-2026/default.aspx

tool_arguments.query: Micron CHIPS Act subsidy US fab construction Q3 2026

events.content: Micron CHIPS Act subsidy US fab construction Q3 2026

**Micron’s CHIPS Act support and U.S. fab buildout**

- The U.S. Department of Commerce finalized up to **$6.165 billion of CHIPS Act direct funding** for Micron on December 10, 2024, to support leading-edge DRAM manufacturing projects in **Boise, Idaho, and Clay, New York**. [[1]]
- In June 2025, Commerce paired Micron’s expanded U.S. investment commitment with up to **$275 million of incremental CHIPS direct funding**, implying total potential direct funding of about **$6.44 billion**. [[2]]
- The original award supports the initial three fabs: **one Boise fab and two Clay fabs**; Micron’s newer expansion plan adds a **second Boise fab** and potentially **up to two additional New York fabs**. [[2]] [[3]]

**Capital-investment commitment**

- At the 2024 award, Micron’s stated long-range plan was approximately **$25 billion in Idaho** and **$100 billion in New York**, or roughly **$125 billion** over two decades. [[1]]
- Commerce said Micron committed to spend approximately **$50 billion by the end of the decade** under the original program plan. [[1]]
- The June 2025 announcement raised Micron’s aggregate U.S. investment commitment to **$200 billion**, encompassing Idaho, New York, Virginia, advanced HBM packaging, and R&D. [[2]]

**Construction status**

- **Boise, Idaho:** Construction is underway on Micron’s first leading-edge memory fab; Micron reported the structural backbone was in place by late 2025 and targets initial DRAM output in **2027**. [[3]]
- **Clay, New York:** The CHIPS award supports the first two high-volume fabs in a planned four-fab leading-edge DRAM “megafab”; each fab is planned with **600,000 square feet of cleanroom space**. [[4]]
- Micron announced its **first concrete pour in Clay**, marking the move from site preparation into vertical construction and occurring more than one quarter ahead of its original plan. [[5]]
- CHIPS funds are not simply paid upfront: Commerce disburses them against completed construction, technology, production, and commercial milestones. [[1]]

**Why it matters**

- The projects are aimed at onshoring leading-edge DRAM—including memory relevant to AI-oriented high-bandwidth memory—and Commerce projected they could lift the U.S. share of advanced memory manufacturing from under 2% to about **10% by 2035**. [[1]]
- Commerce and Micron projected approximately **20,000 jobs** from the original Idaho/New York investment program. [[1]]
